# Dates and Times II

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
```

```{r}
a <- today()
b <- ymd("1941-09-27")
class(a)

class(b)

a - b
```

```{r}
class(a - b)

oski_age_sec <- as.duration(a - b)
class(oski_age_sec)

oski_age_sec
```

## Constructing a duration\

You can make a `duration` by coercing a `Date` object or using a constructor function.

```{r}
dseconds(15)
dminutes(10)
dhours(c(12, 24))
ddays(0:3)
dweeks(3)
dyears(1)
```

```{r}
one_am <- ymd_hms("2026-03-08 01:00:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
one_am
one_am + ddays(1)
```

## Periods\

In `"lubridate"`, a `period` is like a `duration` except it doesn’t have a fixed length in seconds. It tracks human units (day, week) that are responsive to irregularities.

```{r}
seconds(15)
minutes(10)
hours(c(12, 24))
days(0:3)
weeks(3)
years(1)
```

```{r}
one_am
one_am + days(1)

ymd("2024-01-01") + dyears(1)
ymd("2024-01-01") + years(1) # accounts for leap year
```

```{r}
oski_age_sec + dyears(1) # adding average seconds in a year
as.period(oski_age_sec)
as.period(oski_age_sec) + years(1)
```

## Intervals\

An interval is a time span that is tied to two specific, real date-time points: a start date and an end date\
\
Unlike lubridate’s other time span classes (durations and periods), an interval retains complete information about when exactly it occurs on the timeline.

```{r}
# Oski's debute
date1 <- ymd("1941-09-27")

# present's date
date2 <- ymd("2026-03-18")

# interval
interval(date1, date2)

# length of the interval in seconds
int_length(interval(date1, date2))
```

# Time Zones\

```{r}
Sys.timezone() # What R says my timezone is

# names of Time Zones
OlsonNames()
```

```{r}
x1 <- ymd_hms("2024-06-01 12:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")
x1

force_tz(x1, tzone = "Asia/Tokyo")

with_tz(x1, tzone = "Asia/Tokyo")
```
